paragraphs: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he will give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year. In a post on X he called it "the first of many," but he did not say how the giveaway would work, according to CNBC. CNBC said it had asked SpaceX and Musk's family office for details.

CNBC reported that Musk owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, per an August SEC filing. The figure rises to 6.4 billion counting unvested awards and options, a 48.4% beneficial stake. Census data put the number of U.S. children under 18 at 72 million as of July 1, 2025. At Friday's closing price of $146.03, CNBC put the value of the gift at about $10.5 billion.

Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital, founder of Invest America and Trump Accounts, praised the move. He suggested on X that the shares could be distributed through Trump accounts and called it the largest philanthropic gift in history. That is his suggestion, and no mechanism has been confirmed.

The post followed Anthropic's announcement that it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, subject to shareholder approval. Replying to Anthropic on Sunday, Musk wrote, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," and said that is what he would do.

CNBC also noted Musk's record on pledges. It said he gave about $38 million to OpenAI against a promise of up to $1 billion, and did not donate the $6 billion he floated in 2021 for the World Food Program. What to watch is whether SpaceX or Musk explains how the shares would reach children.

Amazon is funding development of a proposed 960-megawatt nuclear plant in Indiana and would be the first customer for its power, the companies announced Monday. American Electric Power would operate the plant, and X-energy, which designs small modular reactors, would supply 12 Xe-100 units, according to TechCrunch.

The plant would replace the defunct Breed Generating Station, a coal plant in Sullivan County near Terre Haute, The Verge reported. Unlike many new power projects, it would connect to the public grid, though Amazon says the power would also serve its data centers. Amazon says the project could create 1,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent roles. The Verge said no construction or operating timeline has been announced and that the deal's terms were not disclosed.

This is the second commercial agreement between Amazon and X-energy, and TechCrunch said it is three times larger than the first. Amazon led a $700 million funding round in X-energy in October 2024, and the two have said they aim to build 5 gigawatts of new U.S. nuclear capacity by 2039.

There are caveats. The Verge described the Xe-100 as unproven and still undergoing development and licensing. TechCrunch said the schedule depends on X-energy delivering its first plant at a Dow Chemical site in Seadrift, Texas, where construction has not begun. The company said its construction permit is in the final phases of Nuclear Regulatory Commission review. Texas has also sued over the site's alleged water and waste violations.
TechCrunch noted that X-energy's shares have fallen by nearly two-thirds since its April IPO, and that experts say mass manufacturing often takes about a decade to pay off.

The Defense Department has signed a framework agreement with BAE Systems to buy up to 25,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System guidance kits a year for as long as seven years, the department announced Monday. APKWS kits turn unguided 2.75-inch rockets into laser-guided munitions. All four services field them, and Defense News reported they have become a cheaper alternative to air-to-air missiles for shooting down drones.

Congress still has to approve and fund the purchase, the department said. BAE said it will raise production while the two sides negotiate a multiyear contract. Neither announced a cost. The framework also outlines a path to 35,000 kits a year for U.S. allies, with that capacity coming online as partner nations request kits through Foreign Military Sales.

Michael Duffey, the Pentagon's undersecretary for acquisition and sustainment, said the agreement keeps production lines running at capacity, provides interceptor inventory and "flips the cost calculus in the taxpayer's favor." BAE chief executive Tom Arseneault said APKWS delivers "proven, reliable and affordable precision at scale."

BAE builds the kits in Hudson, New Hampshire, and Austin, Texas, and said in February that it had delivered its 100,000th. The 25,000 figure matches capacity a company official cited in 2023. The Navy's current five-year contract, awarded in August 2025, is worth up to $1.74 billion for up to 55,000 kits.

Among allies, Saudi Arabia won State Department approval in July for a possible $1.96 billion package including up to 20,000 kits, and Italy is weighing a purchase of 5,031. Defense News called the deal the latest of several munitions framework agreements this year, following ones for Patriot and THAAD interceptors.

President Trump has signed an executive order creating a new division at the National Institutes of Health and a White House task force focused on women's health, STAT reported. First lady Melania Trump announced the initiative Monday, saying, "Beginning today, we will change the reality of women's health."

The NIH division is to be set up within 90 days. Mrs. Trump said it is meant to streamline research into understudied diseases in women, advance diagnostics and improve treatment. It does not replace the existing Office of Research on Women's Health, and STAT said details about it were not disclosed. An NIH spokesperson said the division would work with that office to coordinate research across all stages of life, strengthen the inclusion of women and girls in clinical trials, and increase accountability for considering sex as a biological variable.

The task force, whose first session was set for Monday, will be led by White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Members include Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas and CDC Director Erica Schwartz. The order says the Department of Health and Human Services will pay its administrative costs.

STAT noted that funding for science, and women's health research in particular, has been under pressure since Trump returned to office. Scientists have said their work was put at risk, and the word "women" in grants triggered special reviews at NIH. The administration's response to those claims was not in STAT's report. Trump said Monday that many conditions affecting women remain understudied but "we're studying that right now."

Most of Europe's wild bee species and about half of its hover fly species have declined over the past century, a study has found, according to The Guardian. The results were released as the UN biodiversity summit, Cop17, opened in Yerevan, Armenia.

Records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in every part of Europe except the Alpine region. Bee and hover fly richness fell persistently in the Atlantic and Continental regions, while trends elsewhere were mixed or even positive. The data covers 88% of bee and hover fly species on the continent. The scientists said pollinator communities have been reshaped by the loss of sensitive species and the rise of a resilient few.

Of the species logged over the century, 91% were recorded at least once between 2001 and 2020. That suggests as many as 9% could have disappeared, but many of those were rare in the historical record, and the researchers said they do not expect widespread extinctions to have occurred yet. Species' occupancy, the chance of finding them at a given site, mostly fell.

Lead author Carlos Martínez-Núñez of the Spanish National Research Council said biodiversity loss can hide behind apparently stable species numbers, offering "a crucial opportunity to act." Ainhoa Magrach of the Basque Centre for Climate Change, who was not involved, said earlier evidence came mostly from a few northwestern countries and this work shows the pattern extends across the continent.

The Guardian said Cop17 is expected to assess progress toward this decade's targets, including protecting 30% of land and sea and restoring 30% of degraded ecosystems. It also noted that governments have not met a single UN nature target since 1992.

A Kelvin wave tied to this year's strong El Niño has reached the U.S. West Coast and is raising sea levels, NPR reported. It is a deep ocean wave that forms along the equator when the Pacific warms, moves east beneath the surface, then splits at South America and travels north and south along the coast. Scientists describe it as a planetary-scale wave, not a tsunami or a wall of water.

NPR quoted Dillon Amaya of North Carolina State University as saying the waves do not cause flooding on their own but make it more likely by raising the background sea level. He said levels in Southern California were already six to eight inches above normal in early October when Tropical Storm Rachel's storm surge flooded neighborhoods. In his view the surge was almost certainly made worse by the wave. Warmer water has also brought tropical fish north and stressed marine life.

New Scientist reported that sea level in the eastern Pacific is about 40 centimeters above normal, according to Paul Roundy of the University at Albany. Thomas Monahan of the University of Oxford said his team estimates rises of 9 to 13 centimeters in California. He said the sea-level effect should peak around late November or December, and that long-term lunar tide cycles add about 5 centimeters. The highest tides are expected during Thanksgiving and Christmas weeks.

Amaya expects the next Kelvin wave at San Diego in late October or early November, with more through early winter. NOAA researchers predict El Niño will stay strong into early 2027. Daniel Swain of the California Institute for Water Resources said coastal flooding could be severe or record-breaking, and New Scientist said California declared a state of emergency in September.

Apple has sent invitations to a product launch on Oct. 28, called an "Apple Experience in Los Angeles." According to The Verge, it starts at 1 p.m. Eastern. The invitation says "Pro and tell," which CNBC said suggests a focus on high-end "Pro" devices with Apple's own chips.

Bloomberg reported, per The Verge, that Apple will announce new Macs and a refreshed iPad Mini. The biggest expected item is a MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen that is lighter and has an iPhone-style Dynamic Island. Bloomberg also reported a 14-inch MacBook Pro and a new iMac with the M6 chip, and an iPad Mini with an OLED screen. These are reports and expectations, not Apple announcements.

Melius Research analyst Ben Reitzes wrote Monday that he expects new Macs, including a touchscreen notebook, this fall. CNBC noted that Apple has historically been dismissive of touchscreen laptops. Software chief Craig Federighi said in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users.

The event will be Apple's third under CEO John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook last month. The first covered new iPhones, including a foldable model, and the second, on Oct. 13, covered smart home products, including the HomeView hub. Reitzes called the pace a meaningful shift from two events a year.

CNBC said Apple updated the Mac Mini and Mac Studio in August and refreshed the MacBook Pro in the spring, while the iMac has not been updated since October 2024. Macs made up about 10% of revenue last quarter, and Apple shares are up 26% this year.

Researchers at Quantinuum have used error correction to make their Helios-1 quantum computer store information with the lowest error rate yet reported for logical qubits, according to New Scientist. Logical qubits group several physical qubits together so they make fewer mistakes, and existing quantum computers make many errors.

Helios-1 has 98 trapped-ion qubits. The team used a coding method called color code and, when testing information storage, saw as few as five errors per million uses of a qubit. Similar past experiments saw hundreds. A simple error-corrected operation on two logical qubits had an error rate about 10 times higher, around seven per 100,000 uses.

David Hayes of Quantinuum said part of the gain came from better control of the physical qubits. A special laser pulse now corrects harmful energy shifts, and the color code then fixes remaining errors. The team also showed that errors fell twelve-fold when a logical qubit grew from seven to 19 physical qubits, and again from 19 to 37. This matters because only methods that improve as qubit counts rise can scale.

Steven Flammia of Virginia Tech, who was not involved, called it an impressive advance. He said it sets the course toward a "megaquop" machine, capable of a million reliable operations, and that it remains to be seen whether error rates stay low in more complex operations. Thomas Wong of Creighton University said around 100 logical qubits would be needed for known useful applications, versus roughly 100 physical qubits here.
Hayes said Quantinuum's next machine, Sol, will be nearly twice as large as Helios-1. New Scientist noted competition, including QuEra's plan to build a megaquop machine by 2028.

France imposed partial curfews on Monday after weekend protests turned violent. According to The Guardian, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said after an emergency cabinet meeting that he was "fully resolved to restore public order" and had called for "local and partial" curfews if needed, with "no question" of curfews on entire cities. His office announced curfews from 8pm to 6am on Monday and Tuesday nights in four northern cities, including Lille. Police also set a curfew from 11pm to 6am on two Paris locations, Place de la République and Les Halles.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police "lost control" in some large cities on Saturday and cited a "lack of anticipation". He said intelligence had pointed to 200,000 demonstrators. The Guardian reported more than 500,000 turned out; Fox News cited the Interior Ministry's figure of 550,000 and organizers' figure of 800,000. Nuñez offered to resign, but President Emmanuel Macron refused and ordered a review of planning and intelligence failures. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said, "We unquestionably failed."

Reported damage varies by outlet. The Guardian cited authorities as saying an estimated 2,000 shops were looted, nearly 2,400 people were arrested and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes were injured. Fox News said more than 1,500 stores were reportedly ransacked and that authorities estimate some 3,000 businesses were damaged.

Nuñez said the responsibility of "rioters, looters and ultra-left militants" should not be glossed over. Paris mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said the state "was at fault" and that protests would continue. Marseille mayor Benoît Payan called the situation "almost insurrectional" and described the government's stance as "petty political manoeuvring". Fox News reported that President Trump blamed migration policies, while French authorities have not blamed immigrants, and that Marine Le Pen's National Rally says the government has lost control.
Unions have called for new strikes and rallies on 5 November. Lecornu said a state of emergency could be declared if necessary, but that partial curfews seemed "more appropriate" for now.

The Justice Department announced Monday that it has filed criminal charges against 28 green card holders in California, accusing them of fraudulently registering to vote. A department spokesperson said 21 of the 28 cast unlawful ballots. According to The Guardian, the charges include making false statements in a naturalization application and fraudulently signing up to vote, felonies that could carry five years in prison. Eleven defendants were in custody and arrests were continuing. The charges are allegations.

The Washington Examiner said the cases fall under an operation called "Protect the Vote". It described one arrest, of Omar Alexander Muñoz, 72, a Belizean national, who is accused of falsely claiming citizenship when registering in 2019 and then voting in 2020, 2022 and 2024. Los Angeles County's top federal prosecutor, Bill Essayli, said the arrests "confirm" that noncitizens are voting in California elections.

The charges followed a federal lawsuit against California. The department says it sent state officials a list of about 20,000 people it believes are likely noncitizens who were mailed ballots, and asked the state to set aside their ballots until citizenship is verified. Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter also warned officials they could face prosecution for knowingly tabulating such ballots. Asked about methodology, McCotter acknowledged some names "may" turn out to be citizens.

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber called the demands "outrageous" and said the Department of Homeland Security had earlier suggested 190,000 registered voters might be noncitizens before revising the figure to 20,000. She said treating listed voters as ineligible would violate federal law on removing names before an election. Governor Gavin Newsom said the federal government has no role in running state elections. Los Angeles County registrar Dean Logan said the claims should be settled in court.

The Guardian reported that voting by noncitizens is extremely rare, and that Nevada officials said a similar federal list wrongly flagged 185 people. The Justice Department said it has charged 112 people across 20 states in recent weeks.

Election offices in at least 32 states have received suspicious letters in the past week, according to an investigation by Wired. It began last Tuesday, when an official in the Louisiana secretary of state's office opened a letter and white powder fell out. The office was evacuated and the employee was taken to an emergency room. The employee was not injured, tests showed the substance was not harmful, and the office reopened Wednesday.

Wired said offices in at least 31 other states received similar letters. Most were intercepted by the US Postal Service before delivery, state officials told the outlet. In Arizona, Delaware, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Louisiana, letters were not intercepted and offices were evacuated when powder was found. Officials in 10 states and Washington, DC said they had received nothing, and eight state offices did not respond. The powder in letters opened so far has been reported as not harmful.

Federal agencies warned some states in advance. The FBI told Alaska authorities a package was expected, and Utah officials said postal workers were watching for one. Utah's lieutenant governor, Deidre Henderson, posted an image of an intercepted letter. Its return address listed "DSA", apparently for the Democratic Socialists of America, which has denied any involvement.

The FBI said it and the Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings, some containing an unknown substance. It would not say how many letters it has identified or whether it has leads. Wired also reported similar letters sent to congressional offices, including those of Republican Senator Ted Cruz and Democratic Senators Chris Murphy and Alex Padilla. Representative Hillary Scholten said her letter warned of a coming "civil war" after the midterms.

Election officials said they remain on high alert, with the midterms two weeks away. Henderson said, "Nothing is going to disrupt the midterm election." The Louisiana office said the incident did not affect election operations.

Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar and Republican state House Speaker Lisa Demuth met in their first debate for Minnesota governor, with the state's welfare fraud scandal a central topic, Fox News reported. The scandal, involving pandemic-era social services, took hundreds of millions of dollars, and potentially billions, from federal and state programs, according to Fox. It led Governor Tim Walz to abandon his re-election bid.

Demuth repeatedly returned to the issue. She said, "We have allowed a culture of waste and fraud to go on far too long," and asked Klobuchar why she did not do more and why she missed fraud hearings in the Senate. Klobuchar said, "I would have caught that fraud," and that she called the Justice Department as soon as the fraud became public and asked for more resources, which she said led to more federal prosecutors. On the hearings, she said she has attended a dozen where she raised fraud and that the one Demuth cited was a subcommittee she was not on.

Demuth also pledged to fire "all of the commissioners in the state of Minnesota" to start fresh. She blamed the Affordable Care Act for rising healthcare costs, a claim she made in the debate and which Fox reported without rebuttal from Klobuchar in its account.

Hosted as a business forum by the Minnesota Chamber of Commerce, the debate also covered gas prices, paid family and medical leave, and insulin costs. On taxes the candidates agreed: Demuth said hikes are "off the table" and Klobuchar said she will not increase taxes.

Fox reported that polls show Klobuchar leading by an upper single digit margin and rates the race Likely Democrat. A Republican has not won the governorship in twenty years. Demuth won the GOP primary over Mike Lindell, whom President Trump had endorsed.

A senior adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying, "People [have] already died." The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Ukraine first reported an interruption last week, amid a row with the Trump administration over its deal to import Russian oil. On Monday Zelensky wrote that overnight, one ballistic missile attack on Kyiv came without warning and a second with minimal time to take shelter. In an NBC interview published the same day, he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause and thanked the US.

Beskrestnov said the information remained incomplete and inconsistent, and that the previous night's warning arrived one minute before the attack. He said other intelligence continues to flow and that the problem is solely the air raid alert component. He added that Ukraine has its own radar data for limited warning.

He also said restrictions on Starlink and its military service Starshield continue, with no clarity on who is responsible. Last week Starshield limited the speed at which connected mobile units can move to 100mph, which the BBC said limits Ukraine's ability to shoot down drones or launch mid-range drone attacks. Elon Musk said the US government controls access to Starshield, and Trump has denied involvement.

Beskrestnov said he thought the simultaneous problems were "probably" a deliberate effort to press Ukraine to negotiate with Russia. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no "pause" and pointed to a software problem with the early warning system a few nights earlier. A White House official said Trump is focused on ending the war. Ukraine is looking at alternatives to Starlink, Beskrestnov said.

A Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces in Shabwa province killed at least 50 people, local authorities say. The Guardian and the BBC both cited a preliminary count of 53 dead and more than 200 injured, mostly young recruits. Both outlets said it is among the deadliest single attacks since the civil war reignited. According to the Guardian, three missiles struck al-Alam camp near Ataq while recruits were lined up in formation.

Hospitals were overwhelmed, Shabwa's deputy governor told AFP, and the most seriously wounded were moved to Hadramout and Aden. Yemeni government president Rashad al-Alimi called it a "criminal attack", promised a firm response and asked the UN secretary general to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani called it a war crime, saying the centre was not a military target. A government spokesperson said recruits there were far from the frontlines.

The Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, gave a different account. He said forces targeted "Saudi enemy" concentrations at a camp run by Saudi officers, resulting in dozens of dead and wounded, including Saudi officers. The BBC said there was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

The strike comes amid wider fighting. The Guardian said the Houthis began a push in mid-September to seize the Bab al-Mandab waterway, and that fighting continues around Taiz and elsewhere. Houthi-run media said a Saudi air strike in Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people, while the Guardian reported a Saudi strike killed nine. The Guardian also said an inquiry will examine how so many troops were left exposed.

Meanwhile, the Guardian reported that Egypt's parliament postponed a vote on sending troops to Saudi Arabia, likely until next week. A two-thirds majority is needed, and some opposition parties have signalled they will vote against or abstain.

Iran has attacked at least 15 container ships in the strait of Hormuz over the past 10 days, according to The Guardian. Some vessels were hit by drones and others by mines. On Sunday a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat about 75 miles north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail. Brent crude rose close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.

Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi to Fujairah sank after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew were evacuated and dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating. Rumours that iPhones and other valuable goods were aboard, fuelled by fake AI-generated photos, led fishers and others to search the water. Iranian officials have ordered fishers not to take the cargo, saying it belongs to the state, and a cyber police official warned that salt water can damage electronics.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has the right to attack any ship crossing without its permission or with its transponders off. The UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre recorded 12 attacks in the seven days to 16 October. The Guardian said it is disputed how many ships were hit by mines or IRGC shelling. Two tankers were hit Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels, according to the IRGC, and a third late Sunday. UKMTO counted 254 transits in the week to 14 October, about 70 percent below pre-conflict levels.

On diplomacy, the Guardian reported that Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief. Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov visited Tehran offering to mediate with President Trump, who insists the nuclear stockpile be addressed before he lifts his threat of attacking Iran again. Russia has offered to take the highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to commit.

The newspaper said Tehran is braced for another attack, after Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched a security doctrine emphasising pre-emptive strikes. Researchers also warned of environmental damage from oil and debris.

Benny Gantz, a former Israeli army chief and defence minister, withdrew from Israel's election race on Monday after polls showed his party below the threshold for entering parliament, according to Al Jazeera. The Blue and White leader said he will not run in the October 27 vote and will "continue to work for unity". Polls had consistently shown his party under the 3.25 percent needed to win seats in the 120-seat Knesset.

Gantz, 67, sat in a national unity government with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from 2020 to 2021 and joined the war cabinet formed after the October 7, 2023 attacks. He quit that cabinet in June 2024, saying Netanyahu was preventing progress toward "true victory". Al Jazeera's Nour Odeh said the announcement was not expected, and that Gantz's call for unity refers to a government of Zionist parties, which she said could mean bringing in Netanyahu again.

Opposition leaders, including Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, welcomed the decision as "correct" and "responsible". Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli diplomat, said Gantz's exit is "inconsequential" electorally and politically.

The race is tight. Al Jazeera said recent polling shows Netanyahu's Likud-led coalition locked in a close contest with an opposition alliance, and neither appears on track for a majority. Haaretz's tracker, as of Sunday, showed the Eisenkot-led alliance at 52 seats and the Likud-led coalition at 51. Two Arab-led lists are projected to win 13 seats, though both main blocs have ruled out forming a government with them.

On Sunday, President Trump formally endorsed Netanyahu on Truth Social, writing that if Israel has "the wrong Leader" the US would have to do the work itself on Iran. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera said the endorsement may help consolidate his base but would not solve his coalition problem.

Israeli police said on Monday they had detained 10 people in a rare raid on settlers, after a weekend of violence in the occupied West Bank, according to The Guardian. Police released footage of the operation and said the detainees were connected with attacks on foreigners and the construction of an illegal outpost. Hours later, a court extended the detention of six men linked to the attacks on foreigners to between three and four days.

The raid followed two incidents. On Friday, US photojournalist Heidi Levine was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men while covering the olive harvest in a Palestinian village near Ramallah. She suffered four broken vertebrae, a broken rib, a finger injury that needed surgery and lacerations. She told the BBC the assault amounted to being lynched. The next day, men with sticks and iron bars attacked European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing a car window and severely injuring a young Palestinian man.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu referred to an "alleged attack" on Levine and "unproven allegations" about the diplomats. The Guardian said this disregarded video and witness evidence, and reported that his remarks were widely seen as an appeal to far-right voters before the election. His own explanation was not included in the article. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, ambassador Mike Huckabee, European nations and Washington Post editor Matt Murray all reacted strongly, the paper said.

Levine said the focus on her case showed double standards, since Palestinians face attacks across the West Bank with little done. Yesh Din documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in the three weeks since 27 September. Its director said 94 percent of investigations into settler violence end without indictments. Haaretz reported that commanders are reluctant to confront settler leaders. What happens to the detained men is the next thing to watch.

The UN's World Food Programme has cut the number of people it helps in Gaza each month from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, leaving about 500,000 without support, according to The Guardian and Al Jazeera. The agency says the cuts stem from a funding shortfall, not reduced need. Its funding has fallen by more than half from 2025 levels, and it says it needs more than £300m over six months to restore critical programmes in Palestine.

Other reductions are also under way. Families receiving ration boxes will get one instead of two, with a smaller bag of wheat flour. Daily hot meals will fall from 250,000 to 150,000, and cash assistance will shrink for 75,000 families, Al Jazeera reported. The WFP's Palestine director, Shaun Hughes, said recent gains are fragile. Two-thirds of Gaza's population face crisis-level food insecurity, and 200,000 people are at emergency level, one step from famine. A famine declared in summer 2025 has ended, the Guardian noted, but about 80 percent of people are unemployed, according to UN data.

Hughes said Israeli restrictions on shipments make aid more expensive, and that restoring ration boxes could take about three months even with new money. Al Jazeera reported that aid shipments into Gaza were suspended for a sixth consecutive day after Israel closed border crossings, and that prices for bread and other staples have risen sharply. Gaza's Government Media Office held Israel responsible and urged donors to give funds. The Israeli government's response was not included in either article.

Residents described the strain. Randa al-War said her family relies on WFP parcels and fears famine will return. The WFP is appealing to donors, and whether shipments resume and funding arrives will determine how far hunger worsens this winter.

A Kenyan court has found Paul Mackenzie, leader of a doomsday cult, guilty of murder over the deaths of 191 people, all but one of them children. Justice Diana Mochache delivered the verdict at the high court in Mombasa in a ruling lasting more than eight hours. The BBC reported that 28 other cult leaders were also convicted, while the Guardian said about 30 others were. All had pleaded not guilty. Mackenzie denied forcing anyone to starve, but the court rejected that argument, according to the Guardian.

Prosecutors said Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a sect in which followers were ordered to starve themselves and their children to reach heaven before the world ended. The judge said in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched. Burials in Shakahola forest were called "weddings", she said. Mackenzie forbade schooling and medical care, calling them evil or satanic, according to the reports.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff and bodies were found in shallow graves. More than 400 bodies have been recovered, many badly decomposed, and only 26 were identified, the Guardian reported. Monday's judgment covered 191 deaths, and investigations into the others continue. Gravediggers told the BBC some graves held at least three bodies.

Mackenzie is due to be sentenced on 6 November. He also faces other cases, including terrorism-related charges, which he has denied, and a case over 52 deaths in Kwa Binzaro village, where he has pleaded not guilty. The case has prompted calls for tougher oversight of religious organisations in Kenya. Relatives of victims welcomed the verdict, and one father told the BBC he was happy that all had been convicted.

A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, most of them commuters waiting for rides home, according to The Guardian. The attack hit the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state. A witness, Ahmed Wadi, said he helped bury 50 bodies, including his brother Mohamed. He spoke using a satellite internet connection because of a communications blackout.

Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, at a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after market day. He said 47 other people were taken to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, who asked not to be named for safety reasons, said 30 of them later died. The medic said a separate drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four people who are being treated.

The Guardian described it as one of the deadliest single strikes since the war began in April 2023, when a power struggle between the army under Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, broke out in Khartoum. The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out the strike. All of West Kordofan is under RSF control. The army's response was not reported in the article.

Drones have become more common in the war. Between January and April, they caused at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80 percent of conflict-related civilian deaths. On Friday, drone strikes hit a livestock market in Nyala. The army said it killed RSF fighters, while the RSF said 30 civilians died. UN official Rosemary DiCarlo told the Security Council last week that the warring parties are not moving toward dialogue and that there is no breakthrough on the horizon.

An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, in the country's first cluster of cases, The Guardian reported. The outbreak, the second largest in history, has killed more than 4,300 people and sickened more than 9,000 in the region. Patrick Amoth, Kenya's director-general for health, confirmed the total on Sunday.

The chain began with a Kenyan man who fell ill in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, traveled by road to Uganda and flew to Nairobi on 3 October. He died in hospital two days later, and seven close contacts have since tested positive. Kenya's health ministry pointed to contact tracing and quarantine, with about 108 people quarantined in Nairobi. Allan Maleche of the Kenya Legal and Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids said the tracing seems to be working, but Kenyans wonder why so many lapses let a sick person cross borders.

The Guardian's report focuses on the US role. The US built a quarantine center at Kenya's Laikipia airbase for Americans returning from Congo. Locals opposed it, protests followed, and a Kenyan court ordered a halt. Maleche said the case will be decided in November. Jennifer Nuzzo of Brown University questioned whether the center is the safest option, noting that the US has its own Ebola treatment units. The Trump administration's response was not included in the article.

The article ties the unease to US cuts, including the dismantling of USAID, reduced CDC funding and staff, and US withdrawal from the World Health Organization in January. Senator Raphael Warnock said the cuts weakened outbreak preparedness. Maleche said Kenyans' biggest fear is how other countries will react, especially with travel bans.

Albertans voted on Monday on whether the province should remain part of Canada or begin the legal process for a binding referendum on separation, according to the BBC and The Guardian. Results are expected in the early hours of Tuesday. Officials will count ballots by hand and must finish within 48 hours, with the separation question counted first. If voters back it, a binding referendum could follow as soon as 2027, Premier Danielle Smith has said. Hundreds of thousands voted early, and early figures suggested strong turnout.

The vote followed a petition with about 300,000 signatures from a grassroots group seeking a binding referendum. Supporters of separation say federal environmental policies have held back the oil-rich province and that Alberta would keep more of its wealth as a separate country. Opponents say an independent Alberta would inherit billions in debt, and they warn of lost jobs and investment. A rival petition against separation drew more than 400,000 signatures. Smith opposes separation but says the process lets residents have their say. Polls suggest most Albertans would vote to stay.

The process has been contested. A court blocked the pro-separation petition because First Nations were not consulted, and First Nations groups called Smith's decision to proceed undemocratic and authoritarian. The Guardian reported that the movement has itself been divided, with allegations about some leading figures. It said Smith had estimated the cost of separation at about C$400bn for the transition, and a University of Calgary study said it could cost up to $170bn over five years.

Prime Minister Mark Carney campaigned for a united Canada and called a vote against Canada a dangerous bluff. Separatist Keith Wilson, who published a 214-page transition plan, said the steps needed are doable. A deadly fire at CFB Wainwright on Saturday also muted the campaign. Nine other questions are on the ballot, many about immigration control.

Australian independent MP Helen Haines, 65, was critically injured on Monday afternoon when a car hit her outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, Victoria, according to NPR and the BBC. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said, "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is." Police said they are investigating whether it was intentional. The national counterterrorism team is also involved.

Police said a white Toyota Land Cruiser struck Haines at 3:35 pm. A passerby detained the 43-year-old driver, from nearby Tarrawingee, and police then arrested him. A knife was found inside the vehicle. Police said it is not yet known whether the two knew each other, and they do not believe there is an ongoing threat to the community. The driver is to be interviewed. A witness told ABC they heard a bang and saw a woman pinned between two cars. Haines was taken to a local hospital and then flown by helicopter to Melbourne.

Haines was elected in 2019 and is known as an anti-corruption campaigner. The BBC said she proposed legislation in 2021 for a national watchdog and was credited with helping bring about the National Anti-Corruption Commission. Leaders across the political spectrum, including opposition leader Angus Taylor and Greens leader David Shoebridge, expressed shock.

The attack has renewed concerns about politicians' safety. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said reports of threatening or harassing behavior toward politicians rose from 951 to 1,067 over the past year, and NPR reported more than 1,000 threats in 2025-2026. Albanese said the political temperature has risen and that social media played a part. Investigators are yet to state a motive.

China's economy grew faster than economists expected in the third quarter, helped by strong exports, The Guardian reported. The National Bureau of Statistics said GDP rose 4.5 percent year on year from July to September, up from 4.3 percent in the second quarter. Growth over the first nine months was 4.6 percent, which puts China on track for the government's 2026 target of 4.5 to 5 percent without extra stimulus.

The strength was uneven. Industrial production rose 5.5 percent in September, up from 5.2 percent in August, while retail sales rose only 1.1 percent, up from 0.4 percent. Duncan Wrigley, chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said manufacturing output grew 6.0 percent in September, helped by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos. He also said headline industrial output was lifted partly because coal mines resumed operations after safety inspections that followed a major accident. In his view, policymakers will likely conclude their efforts to stabilize growth worked.

Wrigley said high-tech manufacturing continues to outperform traditional sectors. Data released last week showed exports surged by more than a third in September, driven partly by shipments of AI-related electronics. Analysts at ABN Amro said the pickup mainly reflects export strength from the global AI and tech boom, which more than offset drags from the Iran conflict and weak domestic demand.

The domestic picture remained weak. Fixed-asset investment fell 7.2 percent over the first nine months, property investment dropped 20.6 percent, and infrastructure spending stayed weak. The gap between factory output and consumer spending is likely to remain a focus for analysts.

The United States has ordered artificial intelligence technology from the Chinese firm DeepSeek removed from most government systems, the BBC reported. The Department of Homeland Security has banned all use of DeepSeek within civilian government agencies, along with any technology built with the aid of its AI models. The department made the order public on Monday, but the ban took effect at the end of July.

The order covers civilian agencies, including the Treasury, State and Justice departments. Agencies within the Department of Defense are excluded. The notice did not detail the specific security concerns about DeepSeek. The BBC said the DHS, DeepSeek and the Chinese embassy in Washington had been contacted for comment. Their responses were not included.

The ban follows criticism of Chinese AI from the Trump administration and US firms. White House tech lead Michael Kratsios wrote in an internal memo earlier this year that "malicious exploitation" of American AI firms had occurred, mainly by rivals in China. Anthropic and OpenAI, both expected to list publicly in the coming months, have claimed some Chinese firms, including DeepSeek, essentially copied their models. President Donald Trump has made clear he sees China as the main rival in AI.

DeepSeek is open source, meaning it is free to access and cheaper to use. Its free chatbot app is among the most downloaded in Apple's App Store, and US companies including Snowflake, Vercel and OpenRouter use its models in their offerings. DeepSeek said last year it took about $6m to train its first model, against roughly $100m for OpenAI's GPT-4, a disclosure that sent tech stocks tumbling. Its latest version was released last week, and users have praised it online for tasks such as software coding.

US prosecutors say a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device in a company meeting room had "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing in California reported by the BBC. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, is charged over the device. Prosecutors argue he should be detained until trial as a flight risk. The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.

According to the filing, Alfozan was in "frequent communication" with a member of the Saudi royal family. It also says a Saudi military official paid for a one-way business class ticket for his wife and son, who flew from San Francisco to Doha on 10 October, the day after his arrest. Prosecutors said his arrest came three days before he was due to fly with them from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary. They said his wife told FBI agents her US visa was expiring and the family was permanently moving to Saudi Arabia, as her husband intended to do. Prosecutors argued he has little incentive to stay in the US.

Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for about a year. The company found an audio recorder plugged into the back of a TV in a conference room, covered with toilet paper, on 30 September. A camera placed in the room filmed him on 5 October entering and appearing to look behind the television. The FBI arrested him on 9 October, and his contract was terminated.

The filing says his alleged conduct could endanger US national security because OpenAI executives met government officials in the room while the device was believed to be in place. Alfozan was due in federal court in San Francisco on Monday. If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The FBI investigation is ongoing.

A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using a group of AI agents that mostly worked on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge, as reported by The Verge. Norforge does not name the targets, but Reuters reports that the victims included John Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins.

Researchers found the activity through exposed work on Cairn, an open-source AI platform that describes itself as a "general-purpose problem-solving engine." Users set a start and end point for the agents, which document their progress as they go. Norforge noted that hackers can also use the tool to orchestrate cyberattacks.

The hacker was the "most active" among the exposed Cairn instances Norforge found, attacking companies in the US, Canada, Australia and Japan, according to Reuters. The attacker laid out "preferred intrusion tactics" in fewer than 100 Chinese characters, and successful breaches took about 23 hours, Reuters reported. Norforge found more than 20 exposed Cairn instances that are "likely malicious."

Companies responded in different ways. Cummins spokesperson Melinda Koski told The Verge the company "is investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors." A John Deere spokesperson told Reuters there is "no indication that sensitive information was accessed." SharkNinja said the breach affected a standalone site with product support information, and that it has contained the threat.

Norforge says it is working to get the malicious Cairn instances taken down. Cairn's creator, who goes by @le1xia0, said earlier this month that the platform "was never a 'hacking tool,'" adding that "misuse is a human decision, not a feature of the engine."

The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles has begun notifying people affected by a data breach of driver's license and motor vehicle data, according to Ars Technica. Not everyone whose information was taken will receive an alert. The department said a malicious actor accessed certain records on September 4, 2026, using compromised credentials.

The department said there is "no evidence" the data has been misused so far. It said law enforcement determined the affected information potentially includes driver license and motor vehicle data, including document images, and other personal information. Affected people are being offered one year of credit monitoring from Sontiq, Inc. Because the state may lack current contact details for many former residents whose data was still stored, they can email the department to ask whether their data was involved.

The department did not name the group behind the breach, saying only that an "international cybercriminal organization" was responsible. NBC Miami reported last month on a dark web post in which ShinyHunters claimed the hack and set a September 11 deadline for officials to negotiate a fee. NBC Miami said the group later removed mentions of Florida, which Flashpoint's Ian Gray said likely indicated negotiations. The department did not mention ShinyHunters or answer NBC Miami's questions about the post.

According to the department's FAQ, the attacker obtained credentials from an employee of a local Florida law enforcement agency who improperly stored them on an electronic device. Mitigation steps included blocking unauthorized access, resetting credentials and engaging cybersecurity professionals.

Some residents complained they were notified only this week, more than a month after the breach. The investigation is ongoing, and the department said it will post an update when more information is available.

Japan's space agency JAXA and international partners are preparing to launch the Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, according to Wired. It is set to lift off from Tanegashima Space Center early Tuesday in Japan, which is Monday afternoon in the US. After almost a year of travel, the spacecraft will reach Mars and its two moons, Phobos and Deimos.

The mission aims to answer how the moons formed. Wired reports that some traits, such as the pattern of visible light they reflect, suggest captured asteroids. Their circular orbits aligned with the Martian equator suggest they could instead have formed from debris after a collision between a young Mars and a giant asteroid, NASA's Tom Statler said at a press briefing. An instrument called MEGANE will measure Phobos's elemental makeup. More volatile elements such as hydrogen or potassium would lean toward the captured-asteroid idea, while fewer would support the impact idea.

After surveying Phobos with instruments and a rover, the spacecraft will land to collect at least 10 grams of material using two sampling methods. The goal is to return the samples to Earth by 2031, which would make them the first samples returned from a moon other than our own. Researchers suspect Phobos's soil contains Martian material, which could shed light on how the planet evolved.

Mission leader Kiyoshi Kuramoto said scientists cannot choose a landing site until they have close-up observations, and called returning samples from a Martian moon "a world-first challenge that is not easy." Russia sent three probes to Phobos from the 1980s onward, all of which failed. Team members cited the collaboration among NASA, the European Space Agency and German and French space agencies, and JAXA's earlier Hayabusa and Hayabusa2 sample returns, as reasons for confidence.

Character.AI filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 12, and court filings indicate the move was a key part of a deal with Disney, according to reporting by Ars Technica and Wired. Disney has hired most of Character.AI's staff, including former CEO Karandeep Anand, and may acquire a license to much of its technology, while the startup keeps its legal liabilities.

Character.AI has faced private lawsuits over chatbot safety and investigations from regulators. Its new CEO said in a declaration that bankruptcy aims to reach a "consensual resolution" with personal injury claimants and a group of investigating states. A motion by the company's lawyers says Disney required the deal be "fully consummated" through bankruptcy because of the startup's "diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks." Disney declined to comment.

In September, Disney paid $5.5 million plus a refundable $2 million deposit and hired the majority of employees. Through bankruptcy, Disney seeks a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license to code, tools and other assets, including trust and safety and age-prediction technology. User data and the website are not listed. The license will be auctioned in coming months. If Disney wins and courts approve, it would pay another $12.5 million. Otherwise it gets the deposit back plus a breakup fee.

Disney also drafted an order stating the process should not be viewed as a merger and that Character.AI remains responsible for any liability. John Newman, a University of Memphis law professor and former FTC official, said corporate law safeguards "really weren't built to guard against" such a structure. Experts also worry the deal cannot be easily unwound.
The outlets describe the arrangement as a "reverse acquihire." Character.AI did a similar deal with Google in 2024, and Google was later named alongside it in lawsuits.

CNN's chief international anchor, Christiane Amanpour, has announced she will leave the network next year after more than four decades, the BBC reports. "After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!" the 68-year-old said in a statement.

Amanpour said she looks forward to "interesting new projects down the line" and will keep rooting for CNN and its history of independent journalism. "Remember: always be truthful, not neutral," she said.

CNN chairman Mark Thompson called her "one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere" and said the network will take time to celebrate her before she departs next year. In a memo to staff on Monday, he wrote that she had thought carefully about the decision and that the two had been discussing it for some months. He said he was sorry to see her go but had come to accept that this is the right time for her, personally and professionally.

Amanpour joined CNN in 1983 as an assistant on the international news desk and became one of its best-known correspondents, often reporting on conflicts and wars. She has presented her own nightly interview program on CNN International since 2009.

In her statement she thanked the people she worked with, especially her show teams and field crews. She recalled her first big assignment covering the First Gulf War and later reporting on the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran. "It's the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much," she said.
